description: Hire Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: Find your north star
talks.teaser: Offers career-planning guidance for cybersecurity professionals choosing between leadership, technical, and entrepreneurial paths.
talks.summary:
Steve Winterfeld opens with his own path through the field, from military service and building a security operations center to compliance, banking and threat intelligence roles. A layoff pushed him to plan his career deliberately instead of taking whatever opportunity came next. He then walks through the kinds of roles newcomers can consider, including analyst, incident response, forensics, penetration testing and compliance work, and notes that the hours and stress differ widely between them.

The middle of the talk covers what keeps a professional growing. He recommends becoming a true expert in one area at a time, building partnership skills by learning how the business makes money and reading a company's financial filings, and developing leadership through managing projects, teams or volunteer groups. He also discusses learning habits, such as taking notes, teaching others and using deadlines or paid courses to force follow-through.

For the final stretch, he compares possible end-of-career targets: running a company, staying technical as a CTO, or leading security as a CISO, a role he says increasingly requires board-level communication. He closes with job-search advice: treat the search as full-time work, measure resumes by accomplishments, practice interviewing, and build a support network, since most people find jobs through contacts.

talks.title: Failing Upwards: How to Rise in Cybersecurity by finding (and exploiting) your weaknesses
talks.teaser: Explains how security staff can move into management by quietly taking on work beyond their current role.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that merit alone rarely earns a promotion into management, because managers have little incentive to move a strong performer out of a role they are good at. The speaker separates "failing upwards" from simply surviving setbacks and presents it as a deliberate career strategy that depends on contrast: showing the gap between where you are and where you want to be.

Much of the talk is a personal account. The speaker moves from a help desk job in Tokyo through cloud administration to a platform engineering role in the Netherlands, where, without being asked, they designed a security program from scratch. A new CISO later folded that work into an information security officer role, which became the first step into leadership. The speaker ties the pattern to social-influence ideas: counter-signaling, a bias for action, reciprocity, social proof and likeability. Trust inside a leadership circle is framed as a function of time and exposure, and the speaker argues that small, low-visibility contributions build that exposure.

The proposed method has three phases. First, ease off overachieving and immerse yourself in management culture through meetups and conferences. Second, quietly take on tasks that belong to the next role while still meeting current goals. Third, once accepted, join meetings you were not invited to and openly state your intent, accepting that the answer may be no and that you may need to look elsewhere. The speaker stresses that the approach takes months, suits in-house moves better than switching fields, and carries real risk to one's job. Practical takeaways include building comfort with awkward social moves gradually.

talks.title: Hacking Remote Interviewing: Lessons Learned
talks.teaser: Offers practical advice on preparing for remote security job interviews, from environment setup to handling tough questions.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by a former intelligence officer who moved into civilian security work, treats a remote interview as a test of how well a candidate controls their environment. It opens with the basics: limiting other devices on the home network, keeping the laptop plugged in and the phone silenced, and delaying software updates until after the call. Background, lighting and props are presented as part of the impression a candidate makes.

The middle section covers preparation. Suggestions include a separate account and phone line for job hunting, a clean desktop with the meeting apps already installed, a glass of water, and slow, plain speech. Candidates are advised to review a company's standard interview questions, to check what their own public profiles reveal, and to confirm the role and time zone before the call. Salary negotiation, questions to ask the employer about the job and onboarding, and how to decline unpaid assessment work are also covered through anecdotes.

The closing part warns that job searching from corporate devices can be flagged by employer monitoring and insider-risk tools, and that a recruiter request may sometimes come from a foreign intelligence service. Candidates should follow up after interviews, correct mistakes, and withdraw politely from poor fits. The talk ends by noting that a toxic job is temporary and that leaving one is a reasonable choice.

talks.title: Management Hacking 101: Leading High Performance Teams
talks.teaser: Gives security managers practical advice on expectations, one-on-ones, hiring and building high-performing teams.
talks.summary:
Tom Eston opens by contrasting bosses with leaders and explains how his path went from an early information security role into penetration testing, consulting, and then managing technical teams. He calls management the hardest job he has held but also the most rewarding, and says mistakes, including bad hires, are how managers get better.

The middle of the talk covers practical habits. He recommends a written team charter that states the mission, vision, and role expectations, reviewed every few months so everyone knows what a senior versus junior role requires. He stresses active listening, regular one-on-ones that include personal check-ins and career conversations, and skip-level meetings that can surface problems a direct manager may not know about. For hiring, he weighs emotional intelligence alongside technical skill and looks for energy, intelligence, experience, integrity, and cultural fit. He also sorts staff into top, middle, and bottom groups, arguing that the middle group deserves the most time, and discusses motivation styles and personality frameworks. Coaching works best through open questions and a follow-up summary.

The main takeaways are to set clear expectations, listen more than you talk, protect one-on-one time, hire for emotional intelligence, and invest in the people who have the most room to grow.

talks.title: Penetration Testing Experience and How to Get It
talks.teaser: Gives career advice for breaking into penetration testing through hands-on practice, bug bounties, and networking.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a longtime security professional and trainer, opens by noting that many people doubt they can move into penetration testing without prior hacking experience. He traces his own route from a non-technical job through system administration and application security, landing a pen testing role despite lacking hacking skills. His point is that persistence and passion can outweigh a missing credential, and that a hiring manager may take a chance on adjacent experience.

He recommends building hands-on skills through online labs and capture-the-flag platforms, plus free tools such as Nmap, Metasploit, Burp Suite Community and deliberately vulnerable virtual machines. Basic networking, Linux and Windows administration knowledge and some scripting are useful foundations. Web application testing and bug bounty programs offer realistic entry points, and crowdsourced platforms can provide short paid engagements. Publishing write-ups, CVE findings, scripts on GitHub and talks at meetups helps show employers what someone can do.

For landing a job, he stresses networking, mentors and referrals, noting that most positions are filled through connections, and maintaining relationships over time. He suggests asking contacts to forward a résumé to get past HR screening. In the audience Q&A he also touched on purple teaming and on how someone from QA could move toward application security by learning the OWASP Top 10 and retesting fixed issues.

talks.title: So Who's Line Is It Anyway? (A Recruiter Panel)
talks.teaser: Two recruiters explain how hiring pipelines work and share tips on resumes, outreach, and follow-up.
talks.summary:
Moderated by Kathleen Smith, this panel brings two recruiters together to demystify the job search. Kirsten Renner leads a full life cycle recruiting team for a national security portfolio, while Chris Wright runs a cybersecurity staffing firm. They contrast direct recruiting with agency work and describe how candidates move from an initial screen through hiring manager interviews, panels and clearance checks, with timelines ranging from a couple of weeks to many months.

The middle of the session covers practical advice. The panelists suggest keeping resumes short, tailoring the top section to the role, and avoiding tables, columns and heavy formatting that applicant tracking systems may mishandle. Candidates should prepare questions in advance, ask about the interview process, and request feedback from hiring managers. Relevant volunteer work belongs on a resume too. On LinkedIn, the speakers describe a routine of posting, commenting thoughtfully and connecting with people tied to a target role, while noting that not everyone uses social media.

The closing takeaways stress following up promptly with recruiters and interviewers, thanking them after interviews, and building a network of five to eight recruiters who give honest feedback. Candidates are reminded that persistence is expected and that job searching takes sustained effort.
